notes:
I've written these notes from the pages I could open. My searches and page fetches ran out, so some sections are thin. I found nothing from the Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Orthodox sites, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those sections are left out, as you asked.

---

## Background (for your introduction)

- **When Joel was written: the views differ.** Guzik (Calvary Chapel, close to the Pentecostal/charismatic stream) says many scholars date the book of Joel to 835 B.C. and links the plague to the wicked reign of Queen Athaliah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/ — The NET Bible notes say an early date is possible but none of the arguments used to support it is compelling, and most modern scholars seem to date the book of Joel sometime between 400 and 350 b.c. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Joe&chapter=1 — Ligonier (Reformed) dates it just before the exile, but adds that the book's date bears little on its interpretation. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joel-and-locust-invasion

---

## Verse by verse

**v. 1:** The Pulpit Commentary says "Joel" means "Jehovah is God" and "Pethuel" may mean "the sincerity of God." It treats Joel as one of the earliest minor prophets, before Amos, because Amos borrows from him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Matthew Henry calls it a foolish fancy which some of the Jews have, that this Joel the prophet was the same with that Joel who was the son of Samuel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm
- One commentary on Bible Hub says Joel wanted to be known only as God's instrument, the voice that spoke the word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/1-1.htm
- John Phillips (quoted on Precept Austin): the pen was Joel's but the prophecy was the Lord's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-1-commentary

**vv. 2–3:** The Pulpit Commentary says the elders are called because their memories go back furthest. It hears an echo of the Egyptian locust plague in Exodus 10, including the command to tell one's children and grandchildren. The point of passing it on was to remember God's work, the sin that caused it, and the call to repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Guzik: the plague was so unusual that parents would tell their children they had lived through it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/
- A Precept Austin devotional: because the story carried a prophetic message, it was an important part of the heritage of the people and thus it had to be passed on. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations

**v. 4 (the most disputed verse in the chapter):**
- *Real locusts (the majority view).* Feinberg (on Precept Austin): An actual locust plague had devastated the land. There are no hints in the text itself that the prophet is using an allegory. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-1-commentary — The Gospel Coalition (Busenitz) says the fourfold list stresses how much they ate, and it does not speak of a military invasion. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/joel/
- *What the four names mean.* Guzik reads them as successive waves: chewing, swarming, crawling, consuming. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/ — Yamauchi (on Precept Austin) thinks they are probably stages of the locusts' development, not separate species. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-1-commentary — The Pulpit Commentary disagrees with the stages view. It prefers four species, or poetic names ("gnawer, licker, devourer"). It also rejects the medieval Jewish scholar Kimchi's idea of four plagues in four separate years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- *Reformed (Calvin):* he notes that locusts and similar pests ruining the crops were ordinary events; the judgment was that this went on for years. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/1-4.html

**v. 5:** The Pulpit Commentary: the drunkards were not alarmed by their sin, but losing their wine would hit them harder. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Matthew Henry: It is just with God to take away those comforts which are abused to luxury and excess; and the more delights we make necessary to our satisfaction the more we expose ourselves to trouble. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm
- NET notes: drunkards are the first of three groups hit hardest, then farmers (vv. 11–12) and priests (vv. 13–14). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Joe&chapter=1

**v. 6:** The NET notes say the "nation" is figurative: the locust invasion as viewed from the standpoint of its methodical, destructive advance. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Joe&chapter=1
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees. Kimchi said any gathering of living creatures can be called a "nation," and the word does not support reading the verse as an allegory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Whose land is "My land"? The Pulpit Commentary mentions three answers: the prophet speaking for his people, the people themselves, or Jehovah as owner. Guzik takes the last: God calls the vines and fig trees His own, even in judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/
- The lion's teeth picture the locusts' power to strip all vegetation bare. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/63771/

**v. 7:** NET notes: when the leaves are gone, locusts eat the bark off small branches, leaving them exposed, and it is apparently this whitened condition of limbs that Joel is referring to here. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/download/netbible/ondemand/bybook/joe.pdf
- The Pulpit Commentary gives two readings of "splintered my fig tree": "barked" (the bark gnawed off) or branches broken under the swarm's weight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html

**v. 8:** The Gospel Coalition: the young woman swaps the gaiety of the wedding feast for the sobbing cry of the funeral dirge. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/joel/
- The Pulpit Commentary: she is either engaged and her groom dies before the wedding, or a young widow. Either way her grief is real, not put on. The one being addressed is the people of Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Guzik: Judah should not take this stoically, with false bravado; Joel takes suffering seriously and calls them back to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/

**v. 9:** The Pulpit Commentary: the daily offerings were a visible sign of God's covenant with his people, so losing them suggested the covenant was suspended. The priests also lost their income. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Guzik: the sacrifices stopped only when the food ran out; even Athaliah allowed them. He concludes that the devil is more interested in corrupting true religion than eliminating it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/
- Matthew Henry: a people may be filling up the measure of their iniquity apace, and yet may keep up a course of external performances in religion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm
- Precept Austin: the priests mourned less for their own loss than because they could not give the Lord what was due to him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joel-1-commentary

**v. 10:** The Pulpit Commentary points out the Hebrew wordplay ("field fruitless, land laments"). Grain, wine and oil are named because the temple offerings depended on them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html

**vv. 11–12:** The Pulpit Commentary: the farmers are "ashamed" because their hope has been disappointed. The verse is arranged in a crossing pattern (farmers with grain, vinedressers with vines and figs). Even hardy trees like the date palm withered. "Joy" may mean the harvest that brings joy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Matthew Henry: our own hands are not enough. Even grain already brought home does us no good unless God blesses it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm

**v. 13:** The Pulpit Commentary: grief alone could not remove the disaster, so the priests are called to repent, not just mourn. Sackcloth is the outward sign of inward sorrow. The priests go first because they lead the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Guzik: "gird yourselves" means "prepare to do the work of repentance." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/

**v. 14:** Guzik breaks the verse into steps. The fast says getting right with God matters more than eating; the assembly gathers the people; the elders lead; they meet at God's house; and finally they simply cry out to God and trust that He will respond in mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the fast was the outward evidence of sorrow for sin. The "solemn assembly" was a day kept free of ordinary work for humility and prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- Matthew Henry: Under public judgments there ought to be public humiliations. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm

**v. 15 (the key verse, and where Protestant traditions differ):**
- *Wordplay.* "Destruction" (shod) and "Almighty" (Shaddai) sound alike in Hebrew. Ellicott renders it destruction from the destroyer. https://biblehub.com/joel/1-15.htm — The Cambridge Bible notes the phrase is word for word the same as Isaiah 13:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/1-15.htm
- *Shared view.* Most see the locust plague as a smaller "day of the LORD" pointing to a greater one. Ligonier: the plague is a day of the Lord that foreshadows a greater day to come. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joel-and-locust-invasion — Keil & Delitzsch: each separate judgment is a coming of that day, and a sign of His drawing near. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/1-15.htm
- *Older Baptist/Reformed reading (Gill, Pulpit).* Gill: the locusts were a presage and emblem of greater ones, even of the total destruction of their city, temple, and nation, either by the Chaldeans, or by the Romans. The Pulpit Commentary: Joel's vision reached to the conclusion of the Christian, dispensation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/1-15.htm
- *Dispensational reading* (Calvary Chapel, Constable, Kelly). Chuck Smith ties the verse to famine in Revelation and calls it this Great Tribulation as destruction from the Almighty. Constable: the end-times day includes both judgment (in the Tribulation) and blessing (in the Millennium and beyond). Kelly says the day is when God destroys the beast and the false prophet, or Antichrist. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/1-15.html
- *Calvin (Reformed).* The Jews took false comfort in being God's chosen people. Calvin hears Joel saying God's almighty power will now be turned against them because they provoked his anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/1-15.html
- Guzik: In the ultimate sense, the day of the LORD is fulfilled when Jesus judges the earth and returns in glory. In a lesser sense, a time of judgment as Judah experienced with the locusts and drought is also an example. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/

**v. 16:** One commentator on Bible Hub (name not shown) says the food was devoured by locusts or withered with drought. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joel/1-15.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary quotes Jerome: the sinners' food vanishes before their eyes, and the locust anticipates the reaper. Worship offerings had stopped too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html

**vv. 17–18:** Guzik reads these verses as a separate disaster after the locusts, a severe drought that affected all Judah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/
- The NET notes agree there was a drought on top of the locusts, which had exhausted water supplies, causing life-threatening shortages for animal and human life. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Joe&chapter=1

**v. 19:** Joel himself prays first. Matthew Henry: if ministers cannot move others, they should still be moved themselves and pray hard. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm
- Guzik: God sent them to a place where only heaven could help them, so they would look in no other place. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/
- *Was the fire real?* Guzik speaks of real wildfires on the dry land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joel-1/ The NET notes say the fire here and in v. 20 is probably not to be understood in a literal sense. The locust plague, accompanied by conditions of extreme drought, has left the countryside looking as though everything has been burned up. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Joe&chapter=1

**v. 20:** Matthew Henry: the animals' cry to God shames the stupidity of those who cry not to God in any case. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Joe/Joe_001.cfm
- Bridgeway: God is the one the prophet cries to because he alone can save the nation from total ruin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/1-15.html

---

## Other views

- **Allegory in the early church (v. 4).** The Pulpit Commentary says Jerome, Cyril and Theodoret read the four locusts as four enemy empires, ending with Rome. It rejects that reading and notes that leading Jewish commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Kimchi) took the locusts literally. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/joel-1.html
- **A moral reading.** StudyLight's "Barnes' Notes" entry quotes a moral allegory in which the crawling palmerworm stands for lust and the leaping locust for vainglory. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joel/1-4.html
- **Catholic (Haydock commentary).** It records both readings. Challoner said Jerusalem was four times plundered by the Babylonians, and every time worse than before, but Calmet (whom Haydock follows) says we explain it simply of the devastation by insects. On v. 5 it says the things which you have abused, are now taken away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/joel/1.htm
- **Catholic Encyclopedia on Jerome.** It is frank about his Joel commentary: there are some that are frankly bad, for instance those on Zacharias, Osee, and Joel. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08341a.htm
- **Modern scholarship (NET notes).** Besides the date and the figurative fire noted above, the NET points to the great 1915 locust plague in Palestine as a modern parallel that provides valuable insight into the locust plague the prophet Joel points to. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Joe&chapter=1
